items.title: Johnny Wiggs Interview, 1962-08-26
items.q: Brownlee heard me on cornet and asked me if I'd play in his band, so I followed him.

ctx.x: I just wasn't exposed to the right people. They had them. Tom Brown was playing at that time and Tom Brown could always play well. But I just didn't hear them. The cornet players that I heard around town, I won't mention any names, but they played in the style which we called corny. To this day, people are still playing like that on the west coast. A lot of people are raving about those bands on the west coast. To me, it's still imitation jazz. It's corny. Well, they had many white cornet players that I heard…
Emmett Hardy, no. Some people you know rave about how... I have heard nothing but good about him.

items.title: Johnny Wiggs Interview, 1969-12-14
items.q: Yes, I played with him in Norman Brownlee's band

ctx.x: this. I'm sorry. Very short two-word comment. I'm sorry. Okay. Have you ever heard this, Dick? Well, I hear people say that, and of course, different people have different feelings about it. Some jazz musicians feel that it's not sacrilegious at all to play a hymn, and I think people are very much concerned with their afterlife, and this isn't one attitude towards death, that you should rejoice at it and expect some future life. Many people don't feel that that's a wrong thing to do, to enjoy yourself that way.…

I'd just like to ask Mr. Johnny Wiggs if he has ever played with the musician Leon Rapolo. Yes, I played with him in Norman Brownlee's band when he came down from Chicago after having finished with the New Orleans Rhythm Kings. Harry Shields was the regular clarinet player, but when he came down, Norman Brownlee hired him for these few jobs that I played with him, with Brownlee. Great, great, of course. And need I say that, I mean, his records, it's obvious from his records.
For those people who've heard them, of course, these things are available. Yeah. They are reissued, and it's a shame that more people haven't heard people like, say, Leon Rapolo. Yeah.

items.title: Harry Shields Interview, 1961-05-28
items.q: Well, you know, I hadn't been playing professionally long when I joined Brownlee's band.

ctx.x: Mm-hmm. Are there any other questions, Johnny? Or any suggestions? We still have a couple minutes on this reel. If there's... Anything about any of the old jobs that you can think of or any of the musicians you'd like to ask about?

Well, you know, I hadn't been playing professionally long when I joined Brownlee's band. And when I sat next to Harry, it was the first time that I'd ever played with anybody who really knew what he was doing in a professional way. Harry was a seasoned professional by the time I joined Brownlee's band. And I noticed that Harry played note-for-note harmony for everything that I played on cornet. Now, of course, when you fake, you can never play the same thing twice. It's impossible, unless you memorize a chorus or…

I know, it seems like a couple years ago, you told me, it seems like they were arranging, you mentioned how Harry can arrange pieces and can take his instrument and play the different notes to show the other colors.
